title: 4-round AES-256: one-set last-subkey candidate filter

target.description: AES-256 on 128-bit blocks, reduced to 4 rounds. Lucks includes MixColumns in the final round (Section 2.2 footnote). Equivalent subkey L^r=ShiftRows^-1(MixColumns^-1(K^r)); this is not the final-no-MixColumns convention used by FKLSSWW. The output is a candidate set for the 128-bit fourth-round equivalent subkey L4, not a set of complete long master keys.

setting.key_relation: One unknown standard AES master key; no related-key or known-key access.
setting.key_population: general secret key; no restriction to a weak-key family
setting.plaintext_model: One Lambda1 set of 256 chosen plaintexts varying one byte over all values and fixing the other fifteen.
assumptions: A wrong integral subkey guess is modeled as passing an eight-bit balance check with probability about 2^-8; repeated checks use the source's heuristic filtering assumptions.

time.note: The paper prices the bytewise filter's dominant Step 2 at about 2^20 byte XORs; no conversion to encryptions is applied.

memory.note: The source describes small storage for the four/five-round algorithms but supplies no numeric whole-procedure peak.

preprocessing.note: The paper does not separately price setup for this endpoint.

success.description: Under the intended Square construction, the complete one-set balance filter retains the true equivalent fourth-round subkey L^4 with probability 1: every correct byte guess passes Equation (3). The event is candidate retention, not unique identification, a list-size bound, or master-key recovery. The less-than-2^16 candidate count remains a heuristic mean; the output list has no truncation or early stopping. The existing printed-coordinate conflict remains recorded.

review.scope: Exact-event source proof checked against Section3.1, Equation3 and the complete bytewise candidate enumeration. Probability1 applies to retention of the real L4 in the output candidate set under the intended Square construction, not to a hard list-size threshold or master-key recovery. Existing coordinate conflicts and all full-audit gates remain; no attack implementation was validated.

components.description: Chapter7–13 Eq.(3)/Sections3–6: the necessary balance relation holds under the correct hypothesis in the intended Square construction. Existing ShiftRows/printed-coordinate conflicts mean this is not a certification of the literal implementation.
Chapter7 Section3.1: an incorrect L4 byte passes one balance test with source probability2^-8. Less than2^16 candidate keys is an expectation, not a deterministic list bound.

evidence.interpretation: Correct-event backfill: the original balance proof implies probability1 for retention of the real L4 in the complete one-set candidate list. This is not a probability of unique recovery or of meeting the heuristic expected list size. limitations: Costs and success statements are the authors' analytical claims; no complete attack or third-party implementation was executed.

The general BO definition on chapter p8 omits the previous inverse ShiftRows column adjustment for a nonzero target row. For SR(A)(i,j)=A(i,j+s*i), BO input column j and row k require the previous L byte at (k,j+s*k). The surrounding row-0 constructions avoid this adjustment. Independent finite controls check local algebra, not a complete attack repair.

candidate_space.material: The 128-bit equivalent fourth-round subkey L4; a candidate is not a complete AES-192/256 master key.

count.note: The source's heuristic expected count for L4, derived from roughly two candidates per byte; this is not a measured maximum.

field_conflicts.label: ShiftRows formula and diagram coordinates
field_conflicts.description: Chapterp3 defines left-going SR, B(i,j)=A(i,j+i), but Fig2 and Table1 use right-going coordinates. The later anti-diagonal reaches columns0/2 under the literal left formula and one column under the right diagram. A coherent coordinate convention must be selected before reproducing the printed algorithm. This does not refute the direction-independent integral or establish a standard-key-schedule reflection equivalence.
